description: We’re Down-To-Earth, five friends from Karachi tackling the Lunar Landing Site Navigator. Picture the Moon’s south pole: the Sun skims the horizon, Earth slips out of sight, and mission planners need answers fast. We’re building a tool that turns that tangled data into clear visuals anyone can explore, from engineers to curious students. Big ideas, late nights, and plenty of chai.
summary: Vesper is a free web app for comparing lunar south-pole landing sites. Pick one of seven sites (Artemis candidate regions plus the IM-1 and IM-2 landing sites) and a landing date. Vesper shows where the Sun and Earth sit against that site's real terrain horizon, hour by hour. It also tells you how long the lander has sunlight for power, how long it can see Earth for communication, and how many days the launch can slip before the mission requirements fail. Sun and Earth positions come from the NASA/JPL DE421 ephemeris and lunar libration. Each horizon is ray-traced over NASA LRO LOLA elevation models. The results are checked against JPL Horizons and agree to within 0.006°. At the pole, a few hundred metres or a few days can decide whether a lander survives the night. Vesper turns that geometry into a clear yes or no that mission planners, students and the public can explore and share.
details:
Vesper answers one question about a lunar south-pole landing site: when does the Sun shine, and when can you see Earth? You set a landing date, stay length, how many days the landing may slip, battery hours (the longest night the lander can survive) and the minimum share of time Earth must be in view. Vesper then says whether the stay works. A 360° horizon panorama shows the Sun and Earth moving over the real terrain, and you can play or scrub through time. Vesper also gives countdowns to sunset and Earthset and a timeline of sunlight, longest night, Earth visibility and longest communication gap. A slip strip shows whether the plan still holds if landing slips by up to 30 days. The app also has a shaded-relief map of the pole with permanently shadowed regions, side-by-side comparison of up to three sites, a “Moon vs. home” view against a city on Earth, and a one-page PDF Site Brief. Every view is stored in the URL so it can be shared, and the app works on phones and with a keyboard.

Sun and Earth positions are computed hourly, from November 2026 to December 2027, from NASA/JPL DE421 and its lunar libration, including Earth’s parallax. Each site’s horizon is ray-traced 15 km out in 360 directions over NASA LRO LOLA elevation models (20 m/px, or 118 m/px for IM-1), allowing for lunar curvature. A stay works when the longest night fits the battery and Earth is in view often enough. All heavy computation is done ahead of time in Python with NumPy, rasterio, jplephem and SpiceyPy. The web app is built with React, Vite, D3 and jsPDF and hosted free on GitHub Pages.

We checked Vesper’s Sun and Earth positions against NASA JPL Horizons, and they agree to within 0.006°. The Moon’s frame rotation matches the NAIF moon_080317.tf kernel to 0.004″. Long-term sunlight matches published studies to within a few percent: for example, de Gerlache rim gives 86.6% against 85.6% published. The JavaScript and Python implementations agree to within 0.001°.

Near the pole, the Sun skims the horizon. A distant ridge, a few hundred metres of position or a few days of delay can decide whether a solar-powered lander survives. Vesper makes these trade-offs visible, with a plain-language verdict backed by numbers and every source documented in the app. Earth being in view does not guarantee a radio link, and terrain uncertainty and features smaller than the elevation model are not modelled. Vesper is a planning and comparison aid, not a guarantee of landing safety or mission success.
